commentary_segments.text: Again the noise sources can be combined at the input, in order to be able to compare them to the input signal. The collector shot noise has to be divided by g 2 in m order to be translated into an input voltage. The base shot noise remains where it is. As a result, two equivalent noise sources are found, a voltage noise source and a current noise source, which is actually the base shot noise. Which one is dominant will depend on the source impedance, as we will see later. The equivalent input noise voltage obviously also includes the base and emitter resistances. Note that the expression of the equivalent input voltage is very similar to the one for MOST. The only difference is that now the coefficient of 1/g is 1/2 instead of 2/3. This is small difference m indeed. We cannot forget however that for the same DC current the transconductance of a bipolar transistor is about 4 times larger than for a MOST. Its equivalent input noise voltage will therefore decrease.

This is small difference m indeed. We cannot forget however that for the same DC current the transconductance of a bipolar transistor is about 4 times larger than for a MOST. Its equivalent input noise voltage will therefore decrease.
